solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What township police would need?

blocks.note: the letters run on across the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Asks what equipment a police force in a township would require.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside two consecutive words, and the whole clue is its definition: in South Africa a township is a segregated settlement, and apartheid-era police patrolled them in armoured carriers of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hippo was a heavy armoured personnel carrier used by South African police in the townships during the apartheid years.

clue.text: Cases of hitherto ugly, half-forgotten Hanoverian mares appearing in fabulous horse race

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell around something, so only the outside letters of each word are wanted

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
first and last letters of the word
first and last letters of the hyphenated word
first and last letters of the word
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Ugly old Hanoverian mares, long forgotten, turn up in some legendary horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-forgotten' looks like a halving instruction, but it is just another word to be cased. The Houyhnhnms are the rational horses of Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's Houyhnhnms are an imaginary species of wise talking horses, so a race in the ethnic sense found only in fable.

clue.text: Old man’s audible exclamation of contempt

indicators.note: something audible is heard, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: pa is a familiar word for father, the old man

explanation.surface: A grumpy father's scornful snort, loud enough for everyone to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the old man is heard, and his name said aloud matches the snort.
explanation.definitionFit: Pah is an interjection voicing scorn or disgust, a dismissive noise made at something despised.

clue.text: Russian department closing after student departed

indicators.note: something placed after another follows it, fixing the order of the two parts

blocks.note: a student who has left the school is an Old Boy, OB
closing as in final, the last

explanation.surface: A Russian university department shuts down after one of its students has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Student departed' reads like a student who has walked out, but a former pupil is an Old Boy, abbreviated OB.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblast is an administrative region of Russia and other former Soviet states, comparable to a province.

clue.text: Vessel’s very unusual coupling hooks

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so these letters are rearranged
to hook something is to catch and hold it, so one part takes another inside

blocks.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ship's oddly shaped coupling hooks, of the sort that join railway wagons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship with its coupling gear, but the vessel is a drinking cup and 'coupling' supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A loving cup is a large ceremonial drinking cup with several handles, passed round a table at banquets.

clue.text: Body drawing from biography about girl

blocks.note: a biography is a life story, a life
c, short for circa, means about
lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An illustration of a body, taken from a biography of a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning', but here it is the abbreviation c for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A life class is an art lesson where students sketch a live nude model, drawing the human figure.

clue.text: Brussels throne room turned up treasure

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top, back to front

blocks.note: Brussels is the seat of the European Union
the throne is a jokey word for the toilet, so the throne room is the lavatory

explanation.surface: A royal throne room in Brussels is found to hold hidden treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: The palace picture is a decoy: 'throne' is slang for a toilet seat, and Brussels stands for the EU by metonymy.
explanation.definitionFit: To treasure something is to prize or cherish it, which is what valuing it highly means.

clue.text: Row when entering eg on a fancy here?

definitions.text: Row when entering eg on a fancy here?

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one part is placed within the other
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: to row is to pull an oar, so the oar stands for row
the letters as written

explanation.surface: A row breaks out when someone wanders in on a whim, so it is best avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a place where there is a row if you go in on a fancy is exactly an area you should not enter.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area is a district that people avoid, typically because entering it provokes trouble or violence.

clue.text: Civil engineer incorporating fellow’s jolly design

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so one part surrounds the others

blocks.note: CE is the abbreviation for civil engineer
Andy is a typical fellow, so the fellow's is Andy's
a jolly is a pleasure outing, a trip

explanation.surface: An engineer includes a colleague's cheerful pattern in the plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for the design, but it is the noun: a jolly is a jaunt at someone else's expense.
explanation.definitionFit: A candy stripe is a pattern of bright alternating stripes, usually pink or red on white, like a stick of rock.

clue.text: One holding chair for piano opposite

indicators.note: facing the opposite way means running backwards, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: the whole of the first word and the first letter of the second

explanation.surface: Someone sitting across from a pianist, holding a chair for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano opposite' seems to ask for forte, the musical opposite, and that reading even works as PRO plus F; but the setter hid the answer backwards in the text.
explanation.definitionFit: A university chair is a professorship, so the person holding one is a professor, informally shortened.

clue.text: North Eastern hotel, full up, sadly offering no accommodation

indicators.note: sadly means in a sorry state, so the letters are left in disorder

blocks.note: N is the compass abbreviation
E is the compass abbreviation
Hotel is H in the phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel in the north-east is fully booked, so there are no rooms to be had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offering no accommodation' reads as no vacancies, but it means refusing to accommodate a request.
explanation.definitionFit: To accommodate someone is to oblige or help them, so offering none is being obstructive and not obliging.

clue.text: Absurd sentimentality about distant land

indicators.note: about can mean around, so one part wraps round the other

blocks.note: goo is sickly sentimentality
New Zealand, far off from Britain, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Mawkish nostalgia for a faraway country strikes someone as ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distant land' points to Oz first, but that fails the letter count; New Zealand, NZ, is the far country.
explanation.definitionFit: Gonzo is slang for bizarre or crazy, as in gonzo journalism with its wild, exaggerated style.

clue.text: In private, I agree to receive Republican minister

indicators.note: to receive a guest is to take them in, so one part goes inside another

blocks.note: someone who is in is at home
private as in secret
ay is a form of aye, yes
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Behind closed doors someone agrees to take a meeting with a Republican politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In private' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'in' means at home, and 'private' means secret.
explanation.definitionFit: The Home Secretary is the British cabinet minister in charge of the Home Office, covering policing and immigration.

clue.text: Reserve ready for the match?

blocks.note: surface reading: a substitute player warmed up and prepared for a football game
setter's reading: ready is slang for cash, and something ready for a match is waiting to be set alight

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is British slang for cash, as in ready money, and 'match' is the thing you strike, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Having this means possessing so much spare cash that you can spend it freely and wastefully.

clue.text: Needs about a pound when daughter’s going places

indicators.note: something going is leaving, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: re means concerning, about
a quid is slang for a pound sterling
D is the abbreviation for daughter
sites are places

explanation.surface: Someone needs about a pound whenever their daughter goes out somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the daughter is going, so D leaves the quid. A quid is British slang for one pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Requisites are the things required for a purpose, the essentials, which is what needs are as a noun.

clue.text: Large piece of skin ought to be put back evenly

indicators.note: evenly points at the even-numbered positions, so only every second letter is kept
putting something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A big flap of skin should be stitched back into place neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large piece of skin' looks like the definition, but 'skin' is letter supply; the definition stops at 'piece'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunk is a large thick piece or chunk of something, such as bread or cheese.

clue.text: Company department whose business is first to pick up?

definitions.text: Company department whose business is first to pick up?

blocks.clueFragment: Company department whose business is first to pick up?
blocks.note: surface reading: a division whose trade is the first to recover after a downturn
setter's reading: the staff's whole job is to lift the receiver before anything else

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick up' suggests business recovering, as in an economic upturn; here it means picking up the telephone.
explanation.definitionFit: A call centre is an office where staff handle large volumes of telephone calls for a company.

clue.text: Behold ring being used to bind each type of folder

indicators.note: binding something means wrapping round it, so one part encloses another

blocks.note: lo is an old word for behold
O is ring-shaped
one's being is one's self
ea is the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Look at the ring binder being used to hold each set of papers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ring' and 'bind' suggest a ring binder, which is the answer's sort of folder, but here ring is just a letter and 'being' is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose-leaf folder holds sheets that can be removed or added individually, typically on rings.

clue.text: Whacking small boy could end in outcry

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: Al is a short form of a boy's name such as Alan
might and could both express possibility
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Smacking a little boy is likely to end in a public outcry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whacking' reads as hitting, but it is the informal adjective meaning huge, as in a whacking great bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal intensifiers for something enormous or tremendous, as in an almighty row.

clue.text: Flowers a symbol some mostly abandoned

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
abandoned can mean wild and unrestrained, so the letters run riot

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its last letter gone

explanation.surface: Flowers were once a symbol, but most people have given up on that meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' could be a river in crossword convention; here it is plainly the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: May blossom is the white or pink bloom of the hawthorn tree, which flowers in the month of May.

clue.text: Place such as Washington wouldn’t do for everyone

blocks.note: George Washington, by legend, could not tell a lie
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: A spot like Washington would not suit everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: Washington seems to be the city, but it is the president of the cherry-tree story who said 'I cannot tell a lie'. A U certificate marks a British film as suitable for all.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieu is French for place, used in English mainly in the phrase in lieu of, meaning instead of.

clue.text: The works of O Henry missing from promotions?

indicators.note: something missing from a whole has been taken out of it

blocks.note: taken as written
sales pushes are promotions
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Asks whether the stories of the writer O. Henry are left out of publicity campaigns.
explanation.walkthrough: O. Henry the short-story writer splits in two: the O is kept whole, and Henry is the physics unit H.
explanation.definitionFit: Works in the sense of compositions: an opus is a single musical or literary work, pluralised in English style.

clue.text: Position, say, in which murder committed

definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for the train

blocks.note: to orient something is to position it
to express is to say

explanation.surface: A detective's question: the position, say, in which the victim was killed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example', but it is the verb meaning put into words.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's novel Murder on the Orient Express sets its killing aboard the famous luxury train.

clue.text: Girl climbing a mountain finally needing a hand up

indicators.note: finally means at the very end, so just the closing letter is taken
climbing goes upward, and in a down answer that runs the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: giving someone a hand up is helping them, aid
taken as written
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A girl scaling a mountain needs a helping hand near the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' seems to be the reversal signal, but it belongs inside 'a hand up'; 'climbing' does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: Nadia is a female given name, so any girl called that fits this crossword-style definition by example.

clue.text: Over from a spinner

blocks.note: taken as written
a spinning top is a spinner

explanation.surface: Reads like cricket: an over bowled by a spin bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six balls and a spinner is a slow bowler; neither sense is used here.
explanation.definitionFit: Atop is a preposition meaning on the top of, so above or over something.

clue.text: Demanding return of books: we’re disgusted

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
ugh is the cry of disgust

explanation.surface: A librarian angrily insists on overdue books coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demanding return of books' reads as one phrase, but 'Demanding' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough task is a demanding one, hard and requiring great effort.

clue.text: Who, perhaps, uses it’s elaborately turned out?

definitions.text: Who, perhaps, uses it’s elaborately turned out?

indicators.note: turned out means rearranged, and elaborately stresses a thorough reworking

blocks.note: Doctor Who is a doctor, abbreviated Dr
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone wears it when elaborately dressed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Who is Doctor Who, the television time traveller; the whole clue then describes the formal outfit worn by someone elaborately turned out.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress suit is formal evening wear, what a person uses when elaborately turned out for an occasion.

clue.text: Reading maybe for which one has no time

indicators.note: lacking something means it is not there, so that letter drops out

blocks.note: a unit is one
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Reading is a pastime that some people never find the time for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' looks like the activity, but capitalised it is the English town with a university.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading, the Berkshire town, has a university, so it is an example of an informal uni.

clue.text: One that can suddenly drop a clanger, speaking in cheap theatre

indicators.note: speaking means said out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: when you suddenly understand, the penny drops
a clanger is a blunder, a gaffe

explanation.surface: An actor who might suddenly make a blunder while delivering lines in a low-rent theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The penny drops when the meaning dawns on you. A clanger is British slang for an embarrassing blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny gaff was a Victorian low-class theatre or music hall where admission cost a penny.

clue.text: Ship touring Caribbean’s in race

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all around it, so one part encircles the other

blocks.note: SS is steamship
the West Indies, WI, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: A ship cruising the Caribbean is taking part in a sailing race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' reads as a contest, but it means a people, as a nation is sometimes loosely called.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss are the people of Switzerland, a nation loosely described as a race.
